Part 1: The Data (2 points)¶

We will be exploring a data set on Women's March Madness (Basketball). This adapted data set contains historical records of every NCAA Division I Women’s Basketball Tournament appearance since the tournament began in 1982 up until 2018. Sourced from official NCAA records, the adapted data set captures tournament results across more than four decades of collegiate women’s basketball. All data is sourced from the NCAA and contains the data behind the story "The Rise and Fall Of Women’s NCAA Tournament Dynasties."

The data set can be read in from the following url: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diverse-data-hub/diversedata/refs/heads/main/data-clean/womensmarchmadness.csv

To help you with the analysis, here is a table of descriptions of each of the variables present in the model.

Variable Description
year Year
school School Name
seed Seed. The 0 seeding designation in 1983 notes the eight teams that played an opening-round game to become the No. 8 seed in each region.
conference Conference
conf_wins Conference Wins
conf_losses Conference Losses
conf_wins_pct Conference Win Percentage
conf_rank Place in Conference
division Conference Division
reg_wins Regional Wins
reg_losses Regional Losses
reg_wins_pct Regional Win Percentage
bid Whether the school qualified with an automatic bid (by winning its conference or conference tournament) or an at-large bid. [‘at-large’, ‘auto’]
first_game_at_home Whether the school played its first-round tournament games on its home court. [‘Y’, ‘N’]
tourney_wins Tourney Wins
tourney_losses Tourney Losses
tourney_finish Ordered categories: [‘opening_round_loss’ < ‘first_round_loss’ < ‘second_round_loss’ < ‘top_16_loss’ < ‘top_8_loss’ < ‘top_4_loss’ < ‘top_2_loss’ < ‘champ’]
total_wins Total Wins
total_losses Total Losses
total_wins_pct Total Win Percentage

basketball_tidy <- basketball |>
    select(conf_wins, reg_wins, tourney_finish) |>         # Selecting the rows we are working with
    mutate(tourney_finish = as_factor(tourney_finish)) |>  # Changing tourney_finish to a factor variable
    mutate(made_top4 = fct_recode(tourney_finish,          # Introducing a new binary variable that uses "Yes" for top 4 or higher, and "No" for other variables
                                  "Yes" = "top_4_loss",
                                  "Yes" = "top_2_loss",
                                  "Yes" = "champ",
                                  "No" = "opening_round_loss",
                                  "No" = "first_round_loss",
                                  "No" = "second_round_loss",
                                  "No" = "top_16_loss",
                                  "No" = "top_8_loss")) |>
    select(conf_wins, reg_wins, made_top4)                 # Selecting the final 3 columns that we will be working with (we don't need tourney_finish anymore.)

Part 5: Analysis (34 points)¶

In this section, you will describe your data analysis and perform it.

Task 5.1 Plan out your analysis (10 points)¶

Propose a method that was covered in class that would be appropriate to use to answer your research question. You only need to build one model with one set of predictors in this section. Write a paragraph that explains the choice of method, and be sure to answer the following questions:

  • What method do you plan to use?
  • Why is this method appropriate?
  • What are the potential limitations or weaknesses of the method selected?
  • How are you going to process the data to apply the model? For example: Are you splitting the data? How? How many splits? What proportions will you use for the splits? At what stage will you split? Will there be a validation set? Will you use cross validation?
  • How will you assess the performance of the model? Explain why the performance metric(s) chosen are appropriate.

You answer should be around 250 words or less.

The method I plan to use is k-NN classification. This method is appropriate because the made_top4 variable is categorical (Y/N), which makes classification appropriate. The predictor variables are conf_wins and reg_wins. A limitation of k-NN classification is that it cannot predict out-of-range predictors and it can be really slow with larger datasets. To process the data, I will split my dataset into a testing and training set of 25% and 75%, respectively. With the training set, I will do a 10 fold cross-validation to help select the more appropriate k value, and I will choose k from 1 to 100 by skipping 2. Because I use k-NN, I will standardize the predictor variables before modelling them. Next, I will use the model on testing set. I will then use a confusion matrix to evaluate the model's predictions. Then, I will use precision to assess the model's performance because the number of teams that made the final four is much smaller than the teams that did not. Precision will help measure how often teams predicted to make the final four actually made it.

Task 5.2 Perform the Analysis (20 points)¶

  • Perform the proposed analysis.
  • Be sure to comment your code throughout so that it is easy to follow.

You may add more code cells if needed.

In [41]:
set.seed(23145)  # setting the seed so we don't get different results each time

basketball_split <- initial_split(basketball_tidy, prop = 0.75, strata = made_top4) # we perform the train/test split 
basketball_training <- training(basketball_split) # training dataset
basketball_testing <- testing(basketball_split)   # testing dataset

basketball_recipe <- recipe(made_top4 ~ ., data = basketball_training) |>   # creating the recipe and choosing the predictors
    step_impute_mean(all_predictors()) |> # choosing the mean value for the missing value (acquired from GenAI)
    step_scale(all_predictors()) |>       # standardizing the data
    step_center(all_predictors())

basketball_tune <- nearest_neighbor(weight_func = "rectangular", neighbors = tune()) |>    # model specifications, we set the neighbors to tune() to find the best value of K
    set_engine("kknn") |>         # setting the engine to 'kknn' (nearest-neighbor)
    set_mode("classification")    # setting the mode to classification

k_vals <- tibble(neighbors = seq(from = 1, to = 100, by = 2))  # creating different possible values for k to test them

basketball_vfold <- vfold_cv(basketball_training, v = 10, strata = made_top4) # creating 10 fold cross-validations

basketball_possible_ks <- workflow() |>       # fitting the model using workflow and the recipe and model specs from earlier
    add_recipe(basketball_recipe) |>
    add_model(basketball_tune) |>
    tune_grid(resamples = basketball_vfold, grid = k_vals) |>  # trying different values of K on 10 cross-validations to find the best one
    collect_metrics()    # creating the table of results for each value of k
  
accuracies <- basketball_possible_ks |>   # finding the best K through the highest mean value (accuracy)
    filter(.metric == "accuracy")

best_k <- accuracies |>
    arrange(-mean) |>
    slice(1) |>
    pull(neighbors)

best_k   # so the best value for K from 1 to 100 is 9.
9
In [43]:
# now we train our model using K = 9

best_spec <- nearest_neighbor(weight_func = "rectangular", neighbors = best_k) |>    # model specifications with the best K
    set_engine("kknn") |>         # setting the engine to 'kknn' (nearest-neighbor)
    set_mode("classification")    # setting the mode to classification

basketball_fit <- workflow() |>   # fitting the model on training dataset using K = 9 using the recipe and the best_spec
    add_recipe(basketball_recipe) |>
    add_model(best_spec) |>
    fit(data = basketball_training)

basketball_fit

Task 5.3 Create a Visualization or Table of the Results of your Analysis (4 points)¶

  • Create a visualization or table that is relevant to the results of your analysis (comment your code throughout so that it is easy to follow).
  • Describe what this visualization or table is showing, and why it is important to the analysis (approx 150 words or less).

  1. The first graph shows the Accuracy changes as the Number of Neighbors increases, and we can see that accuracy rises quickly for small values of K and reaches its heighest at K = 9, with an accuracy of ~93%. After that point, the accuracy remains stable or decreases slightly. Therefore, K = 9 was selected as the optimal value in the model specs because it gives the best performance. This graph is important because it helps choose the best K, which maximizes model's accuracy.

  2. The confusion matrix shows that the model correctly predicted 486 teams that did NOT make it to the top 4, and 5 teams that made it to the top 4. The model only made 2 false positive predictions. So the precision score is 5 / (2 + 5) * 100 = 71.4% meaning that in 71.4% of the cases, the model is estimated to predict made_top4 as "Yes" correctly, which shows that the model is reasonably good but not perfect. The confusion matrix is important because it shows how reliable the model is when predicting that a team will finish in the top 4.

Part 6: Discuss your Results (10 points)¶

In this section, you will discuss some interesting findings from your analysis in Part 5

Task 6.1: Discuss your findings (10 points)¶

In 1 to 2 paragraphs (approx. 300 words or less):

  • Summarize what you found from the analysis in Part 5, in relation to your research question of interest.
  • The data science workflow is an iterative process. Discuss if at any point you had to adjust your analysis plan based on the results.
  • Discuss whether this is what you expected, or if anything was surprising.
  • Discuss the impact of the results, and what future questions this could lead to.

For my analysis, I used a K-nn classification model to determine whether conference and regional wins could predict if a team would make the final four in the tournament. After using a 10 fold cross-validation, the best value of k that I found was 9. To evaluate the model's performance, precision was used because there was a massive imbalance among the made_top4 factors. My final model had a precision of 71.4%, which means that the model correctly predicts whether a team would make the final four (Yes for the made_top4) 71.4% of the times. This shows that conference and regional wins are useful predictors for my research question, however they aren't perfect predictors for every outcome.

My results were aligned with my expectations because I predicted that the teams with more conference and regional wins would be stronger teams and make the final four more often. I didn't have an major changes to my analysis plan because the K-nn classification model, confusion matrix, and the precision analysis worked well for answering my research question. My findings suggest that conference and regional performance are important for predicting whether a team will make the final four in the tournament. Future research can examine if there are any additonal predictors (e.g. first_game_at_home) that can strengthen the model's performance to better predict if a team will make the final four in the tournament.
